limitations: Nothing here has been printed, handled or played. The fits, wall thicknesses and overhang margins are measurements taken on the exact CAD solids and predictions for a 0.4 mm nozzle at 0.2 mm layers.

The verification pipeline ran for 769.71 s and did NOT finish every check. 51 of its 52 geometry checks passed and one was left unverified: the wall-thickness gate on part_world_venus_sol, which the shared 600-second geometry allowance ran out on as the 83rd and last step of the run. An interrupted check has no verdict, so no passing result is inferred from it and this build is handed over as an unverified prototype. What did pass, measured in this run: all 24 printed parts cleared the mesh gate and the 45-degree overhang gate at a 0.4 mm nozzle; 23 of the 24 cleared the wall-thickness gate at that nozzle, the exception being the one named above; the 186-occurrence assembly validates and inspect interfere reports clashCount 0 over 298 boolean-tested pairs; and check_fit, check_layout and both spec checks returned clean. Both corrected Mercury parts are among those that passed every gate, with 0 unsupported overhang samples over 0 regions each. See GEOMETRY-NOTES.md and measure/verification-pipeline.md.
Motion verification is switched off for this build and is recorded as unverified rather than passed. Nothing in the set moves relative to anything else in any case.

Mercury is the one world in the set that takes three filaments -- gray, cocoa brown and white -- where every other world takes one or two beyond its globe. The reason is measured rather than assumed. On this 13.78 mm globe, the smallest in the set, the dark grey the plains used to carry is 21.8 of 255 greyscale levels away from the grey globe it sits on when both are rendered at the frames the product is photographed from, and at that separation the patches are simply not visible. Cocoa brown measures 45.5 on the same test and the basin's white floor 36.9 against the globe and 114.3 against the rim around it. Black separates furthest of all at 139.6 and was deliberately not used: a black patch on a small grey ball reads as a hole in the print rather than as terrain. measure/mercury-tone-separation.md is the measurement, taken by rendering the same piece twice at one camera with only the filament changed.

What the cocoa brown costs is that it is a warm brown rather than a neutral grey, so at a glance Mercury's plains sit in the same family of colour as Mars's dark continents and Saturn's and Jupiter's bands. That is the price of the separation above and it was paid deliberately; the neutral alternative is the tone this revision exists to replace.

Mercury's plains are drawn from a formula rather than from a map. Its albedo boundaries are genuinely soft and its plains are genuinely unnamed, so there is no silhouette anyone could check the model against, and the rings are generated deterministically as lobed regions on the seven centres the set already used. What they claim is that Mercury's surface is smooth plains of unequal shape that run together, not that any particular plain is anywhere in particular.

The Caloris basin's size and latitude are real -- about 1550 km across on a planet 4879 km in diameter, which is 36 degrees of arc and 4.33 mm here, at latitude 30 north. Its longitude is not: this set fixes no meridian on Mercury, so the basin was placed at 50 degrees west because that is where it faces both photographed frames most squarely. That is a camera decision and is stated as one.

No crater field was added to Mercury, and the number rather than the opinion: one degree of arc is 0.120 mm on this globe, so a 0.4 mm nozzle is 3.33 degrees and the largest crater outside Caloris subtends three to six degrees -- one or two nozzle widths, with no room for a rim and a floor inside it. It would print as a pit one extrusion wide and read as a print defect, and the set's material rules forbid deliberate grit. Caloris is the exception precisely because at 36 degrees of arc it is eleven nozzle widths across. Nothing else the reference shows and this globe does not carry: no relief anywhere, and no fourth filament.

One of Mercury's seven plains was simplified: the southern lead plain is drawn at a mean 20 degrees of angular radius rather than 22 and biased north, because at 22 its southern boundary ran past the parallel where the seat cone springs and the visible sphere ends. Its centre did not move, and it now leaves 0.53 mm of visible grey between the plain and the seat. Nothing else on Mercury was simplified and no patch was dropped; every ring, channel and annulus is listed in measure/mercury-atlas-resolution.md.

Mars's dark markings are the classical albedo map at the accuracy an eyepiece sketch has, not spacecraft mapping. Four vertices were moved to clear the nozzle on a 14.72 mm globe where one degree of arc is 0.128 mm: three of them close threads of red too narrow to print where the southern seas are meant to run together, and one opens a channel between Sinus Sabaeus and Sinus Meridiani that was too narrow to keep. None of them moves an outline the eye reads. Sinus Sabaeus, the thinnest feature on the globe, is carried exactly as drawn at a measured narrowest width of 0.85 mm. Every ring, channel and join is listed in measure/mars-atlas-resolution.md.

Mars's albedo is cocoa brown on a red globe, and those two filaments are only 1.88:1 apart in contrast -- under the 3:1 at which a difference in value reads as darkness rather than as a change of colour. The brown is genuinely the darker of the two, but at a glance the markings read as a colour change more than as shading. Mars was required to keep exactly red, cocoa brown and white, so this is stated rather than fixed.

The review renders in the CAD project's snap/ folder are drawn by a tool that encodes colour twice, so in those images Mars's cocoa brown appears as a light ochre and looks lighter than the globe, and Mercury's plains and Caloris rim do the same. The colours sealed on the parts themselves are the catalogue values and are what a printer and a listing read. measure/filament-value.md measures both ends of it, and measure/mercury-tone-separation.md reports every Mercury separation on the sealed channels as well as in the rendered pixels. Every visual judgement in this build, the blind review included, was made on double-encoded images; that is a limitation of this build's evidence.

Mars's globe is sunk 2.00 mm into its disc and cut level with it, which at Mars's axial tilt removes about a seventh of the sphere and almost all of the south polar cap. The northern cap is the larger and more irregular of the two and that is measurable in the geometry, but it is not visible on the finished piece and is not claimed to be.

Nothing was added to Mars that the reference does not show: no craters -- at this size a crater reads as a print defect -- no Olympus Mons, no Valles Marineris, no Hellas, no bright highlands and no fourth filament.
Earth and Neptune share the same blue filament. They are 5.19 mm apart in globe diameter, Earth carries green land and Neptune does not, and they carry different rank numerals.
The low side of Saturn's ring is thickened where its underside is carried down to the disc. That is what lets a tilted ring print without support, and it is visible from a seated eye.

The star's two flames are slimmer than the design that was handed in. That design stood them on Ø11.00 feet hanging outside the star's own cell, and the overhang check measured 53 mm² and 52 mm² of unsupported material under them with 9 mm of air below. The feet were narrowed to Ø6.00 and brought inboard so each flame stands on solid flange and prints without support; their 18 mm height, their outward lean and their taper are unchanged.

Earth's globe is 16.70 mm across, where one degree of arc is 0.15 mm against a 0.4 mm nozzle. Every coastline, sea channel and desert edge was measured against that, and one was moved to clear it: the Australian outback's north-west corner came 0.33 mm inland, which would otherwise have left a strip of green too thin to print. Nothing else was simplified and no landmass was dropped.

Earth's coastlines are a stylised silhouette atlas, not a survey coastline. Central America is one broad land bridge, and Japan, New Zealand, the Indonesian and Philippine arcs, the British Isles as a shape of their own, the Mediterranean's islands and Antarctica are not drawn; most are narrower than a 0.4 mm nozzle on a Ø16.70 globe, and each is listed with its reason in measure/earth-atlas-resolution.md. Nothing was dropped silently.

Earth's beige dryland is #F7E6DE, a very pale warm white. At this globe size it sits close in value to the white ice, and an unlit reader of the renders calls it light grey rather than sand. Both filaments were required to stay, so this is stated rather than fixed.

The small desert rings are simple polygons at this size -- inner Asia has seven vertices, the American southwest six -- and read as blocks. The atlas draws deserts as blocks and coastlines as coastlines; only the coastlines carry the recognition.
Geometry inspection is incomplete. This prototype is unverified and is not print-ready; see GEOMETRY-NOTES.md.
product.summary: Jungle Chess played with the solar system. Every piece is a planet, and a planet's size on the board is the fifth root of its real measured diameter, so rank is something you can see rather than something you have to learn: Mercury is the smallest world in play and Jupiter the largest, and the traditional rules are followed exactly as written. Matter faces antimatter. One army's worlds lean their poles one way and the other army's lean the other, by each planet's own true axial tilt, and the bases give the same answer again in white against black. Five of the eight worlds wear the pattern a telescope shows as circles and bands. Earth wears its own coastlines, Mars its own dark continents -- Syrtis Major, the wedge every telescope owner has drawn since 1659, is a triangle here rather than a dot, and the southern seas run together into one dark belt -- and Mercury its own smooth plains with the Caloris basin sitting on the face you photograph, a bright floor inside a raised rim. Those three are the worlds in the set with a surface a telescope really maps. A cocoa-brown asteroid belt crosses the middle of the field, a star stands at each end with two flames bursting off the board edge, and the three cells around each star are sunken corona wells where a captured world drops out of the light and its rank counts for nothing. You win by walking one of your worlds onto the rival star.
product.title: Antisol Caloris
product.what_arrives: Forty-two printed parts: sixteen worlds, a board in four panels, twelve asteroid-belt tiles, two stars, six corona cells and two storage trays. Nothing is glued, screwed or assembled; the tiles and stars drop into their own pockets and the panels butt together.
